title: Shrimp and Grits
subtitle: prawns in bacon cream sauce on soft grits
excerpt: Creamy, buttery grits topped with prawns in a bacon and cream sauce. This is a low-country Southern dish that works for brunch, lunch, or dinner. It comes together in under 30 minutes.
sourceNotes: Shrimp and grits is a cornerstone of South Carolina low-country cooking. It was once fisherman's breakfast food. A 1985 article in the New York Times helped bring it national attention.

content.text: Start the grits first -- they take longer than the prawn sauce. Stir them often to prevent sticking. The grits should be soft and creamy, not stiff.
Bring 600ml water and the milk to a simmer in a saucepan. Add the salt.
Pour in the grits in a steady stream, stirring constantly. Cook over low heat for 15 minutes, stirring often, until thick and creamy.
Stir in the butter. Keep warm with a lid on.
In a frying pan over medium heat, cook the bacon until crisp. Remove and set aside.
Add the garlic and spring onion to the bacon fat. Cook for 1 minute.
Add the prawns. Cook for 2 minutes until pink. Pour in the stock and cream.
Simmer for 2 minutes until the sauce thickens slightly. Add lemon juice and the bacon back in.
Spoon grits into bowls. Top with the prawn sauce and serve immediately.

items.cause: Cooked too fast or not stirred enough
items.fix: Add a splash of hot water and stir vigorously over low heat. Grits thicken as they cool, so serve quickly.

items.cause: Overcooked -- prawns only need 2 to 3 minutes
items.fix: Remove them as soon as they curl and turn pink. They continue cooking in the hot sauce.

items.cause: Too much stock or not reduced enough
items.fix: Simmer the sauce for an extra 2 minutes without the prawns before adding them back in.

content.text: Shrimp and grits comes from the low-country region of South Carolina and Georgia, where both prawns and corn have long been staple ingredients. Fishermen ate it as a simple morning meal long before it appeared on restaurant menus. Food writer Craig Claiborne's 1985 piece in the New York Times introduced it to a wider audience. It is now a fixture on menus across the American South.
